keep: The idea is named up front: random error shrinks with repeats, a steady offset does not, so a result is a value plus or minus its uncertainty.

The picture is the brief's offset and repeats: fifty simulated float-voltage readings of an example 27.00 V battery bank, 0.04 V of random error, beads the mean of 1, 2 or 4 readings, the 'Meter reads high by' slider inside an example ±(0.1% + 2 digits) window, the 0.01 V | 0.05 V meter making bricks, and the adapted last screen with an example limit at 27.02 V.

Worked numbers computed from shown rules: 0.04 ÷ √4 = 0.02 V; 2 × 0.04 ÷ √50 ≈ 0.011 V; 2 × 0.02 ÷ √50 ≈ 0.006 V; 0.027 + 0.02 = 0.047 V; 1% of 50.0 V plus three 0.1 V digits gives 49.2 to 50.8 V; the practice example's 26.97 to 27.11 V against 27.15 V.

Each brief misconception has a DO with its own hint: one reading is the answer (screen 2), averaging fixes everything (screen 10), precision for accuracy (screens 8 and 13), result read as where readings land (screen 6), dividing by n (screen 4's 0.01 V), a pass called on an overlapping bracket (screen 12).
Thirteen screens alternate SHOW (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) and DO (2, 4, 6, 8, 10), ending with two mixed puzzles (12, 13).

Four footnotes, each on a rule or value he might look up; the factor of 2 for about 95% is put as 'textbooks add', since no kept source states it. The overlap rule is reasoned from the bracket, not cited. No source is named in the text.
Analogy from his own kit: a tape with a bent hook, with where it breaks (a percentage part, hidden offset).
fix: Causal step skipped: why the spread falls by √n and not by n. Say the errors are random, so they cancel only partly, never fully.
False absolute: 'No single reading is the true value.' One reading can land on it by chance. Say no single reading can tell you the true value.
False absolute: 'Every reading carries two kinds of error.' Say a reading can carry two kinds.
False absolute: 'A stated uncertainty always needs both parts' and 'Only a check against a known reference finds the offset.' Drop 'always'; say a check against a known reference is what finds it.

Order of claims in the limit paragraph: it says a bracket wholly one side shows a pass or fail before saying the repeats' bracket is only the random part. True only of a full uncertainty. Put the full uncertainty first, then the rule.

Screen 11: 'At 0 and 0.01 V the whole result bracket sits below the limit' depends on the batch. Say the opening batch is picked so, and keep the fail case honest: the true value stays under the limit, so the 'fail' at 0.03 V is the offset's doing.
Practice: link the course's hook. A rise between two single readings means little until it is set against each reading's bracket. Add one common mistake.
